gallery.filename: Airfield Birdman of RAF Lossiemouth - geograph.org.uk - 732855.jpg
gallery.title: File:Airfield Birdman of RAF Lossiemouth - geograph.org.uk - 732855.jpg
gallery.description: Airfield  Birdman of RAF Lossiemouth Originally a Royal Navy base known as HMS Fulmar, the airfield always had and still has to the present day a BCU or Bird Control Unit. The idea was to lessen the chances of aircraft bird-strikes at this busy flying base and when it was handed over to the RAF in 1975 to become RAF Lossiemouth, the BCU stayed in residence.  Here, falconer, Chris is putting a Peregrine through its paces on the airfield using a "lure" on a piece of string. In the distance you can see the Air Traffic Control tower and some hangars.
categories: Images from Geograph Britain and Ireland

gallery.filename: "Flaps, undercarriage, power on, going round again" - geograph.org.uk - 1568376.jpg
gallery.title: File:"Flaps, undercarriage, power on, going round again" - geograph.org.uk - 1568376.jpg
gallery.description: "Flaps, undercarriage, power on; going round again!" A Tornado of RAF Lossiemouth overshoots runway 05. The number 05 originates from the magnetic direction of the runway i.e. 050 degrees magnetic. So when you hear them talk of Heathrow's runway 28 then you'll know that the runway almost runs east-west. Can you see the navigation/anti collision lights on the Tornado? Red for port and green for starboard it is; but which is right and left? The old school RAF teaching used the formula, "There's no red port left!" That's enough military secrets for one night and besides I don't think I really ought to be in this field!
categories: Images from Geograph Britain and Ireland

gallery.filename: "Turning finals with three greens for runway 05 to roll." - geograph.org.uk - 1568300.jpg
gallery.title: File:"Turning finals with three greens for runway 05 to roll." - geograph.org.uk - 1568300.jpg
gallery.description: "Turning finals with three greens for runway 05 to roll." A Tornado aircraft of RAF Lossiemouth doing circuits at dusk. Aircrew have to practise various forms of airfield approaches on a monthly basis to keep their flying categories current. Approaches can be full radar approaches where the aircraft is talked down by air traffic control or approaches can be executed solely by the crew using internal instruments. "Three greens" refers to the three green lights which confirm that the landing gear is down and locked and "roll" is where the aircraft touches down and applies power to go around again. This procedure in RAF parlance is called "circuits and bumps"!
categories: Images from Geograph Britain and Ireland

gallery.filename: Illuminations, natural and unnatural on Runway 05^ - geograph.org.uk - 1568317.jpg
gallery.title: File:Illuminations, natural and unnatural on Runway 05^ - geograph.org.uk - 1568317.jpg
gallery.description: Illuminations, natural and unnatural on  Runway 05! If the pilot sees the runway from this angle then he is in dire straits! He is much too low and unlike the computer version he will not have a second chance. The brightness of the moon will not help him either. Note the runway caravan to the port side of the runway threshold. The number designated to a runway as seen here denotes the magnetic direction in which the landing strip runs i.e. 050 degrees. Heathrow runway 28 would therefore run 280 degrees or almost east west.
categories: Images from Geograph Britain and Ireland

gallery.description: Looking Towards Balgreen Balgreen is right beside the perimeter of RAF Lossiemouth, at the far end of this partly flooded field.
